title: A range that catches the truth
objectives: Build a 95% confidence interval and say exactly what the 95% means.

screens.prose: A backtest's average daily return $\bar X$ is close to normal around the true mean $\mu$. Measured in standard errors from $\mu$, it follows $N(0, 1)$. Slide $z$ to widen the shaded band, from $-z$ to $z$.

params.xLabel: Distance of $\bar X$ from $\mu$, in standard errors

screens.question: Find the $z$ at which the band holds 95% of sample means.

hints.text: Watch the probability label as the band widens.
One standard error each side holds about 68%. You need more.
The label reads 0.95 at $z = 1.96$.

feedback.correct: At $z = 1.96$ the band holds 95% of sample means.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep sliding until the label reads 0.9500.

byKey.one-se: One standard error each side holds 68%. Widen the band further.
byKey.ninety: Near 1.645 the band holds 90%. Widen it a little more for 95%.
byKey.two: Two standard errors hold 95.45%, slightly more than 95%. The exact multiplier is 1.96.
byKey.ninety-nine: Near 2.576 the band holds 99%. Narrow it back for 95%.

explain.text: You widened the band until it held 0.95, at $z = 1.96$. So $P(|\bar X - \mu| \le 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}) = 0.95$. Read the other way round: in 95% of samples, $\mu$ sits within 1.96 SE of $\bar X$.

screens.prose: Flip it round. In 95% of samples, $\mu$ lies within $1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$ of $\bar x$. So the range $\bar x \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$ is a **95% confidence interval** for $\mu$. A backtest gives $\bar x = 0.12\%$ a day, with $\mathrm{SE} = 0.05\%$.
screens.question: What is the lower end of the 95% interval, in %?

hints.text: Start at $\bar x$ and step down.
The interval is centred on $\bar x = 0.12$.
Step down $1.96 \times 0.05 = 0.098$ from 0.12.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}$ from $\bar x$.

byKey.one-se: You stepped down one SE. That interval catches $\mu$ only 68% of the time.
byKey.two-se: You used 2 SE. Close, but the 95% multiplier is 1.96: $0.12 - 0.098 = 0.022$.
byKey.raw-z: You subtracted 1.96 itself. Multiply it by the SE first.
byKey.decimal: 0.00022 is 0.022% written as a decimal. The field asks for the number of per cent, so type 0.022 without a % sign.

explain.text: $0.12 - 1.96 \times 0.05 = 0.022$, and the upper end is $0.12 + 0.098 = 0.218$. The interval is centred on $\bar x$, which we see, not on $\mu$, which we never see.

screens.prose: Now test the claim. A strategy truly earns $\mu = 0.05\%$ a day, with daily sd 1%. Each line is one 100-day backtest's interval, $\bar x \pm z \times 0.1\%$. Lines that miss $\mu$ turn orange.
screens.question: Set $z = 1.96$. How many of the 100 intervals miss $\mu$?

widget.accept: 5 of these 100. The long-run share is exactly 5%.
widget.label: Intervals that miss

hints.text: Slide the multiplier up to 1.960 and read the caption.
The orange lines are the misses.
At $z = 1.96$ the caption counts the orange lines: 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $z$ to 1.960, then count the orange lines.

byKey.hits: 95 is the number that catch $\mu$. Count the orange ones, which miss.
byKey.none: Some lines still miss at 1.96. Check that the slider reads 1.960.

explain.text: At $z = 1.96$, 5 of these 100 intervals miss $\mu$. Over more and more backtests, the share that miss converges to exactly 5%. That long-run share is what the 95% describes.

screens.prose: Same 100 backtests. A 90% interval uses the multiplier $z = 1.645$, so each line gets shorter.
screens.question: Slide down to $z = 1.645$. How many intervals miss $\mu$ now?

widget.accept: 10 of these 100. The long-run share is exactly 10%.
widget.label: Intervals that miss

hints.text: Shorter lines reach less far, so more of them miss.
Set the slider to 1.645 and read the caption.
At $z = 1.645$ the caption reads 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $z$ to 1.645 and count the orange lines.

byKey.same: 5 was the count at 1.96. Move the slider down to 1.645 first.
byKey.hits: 90 is the number that catch $\mu$. Count the misses.

explain.text: At $z = 1.645$, 10 of the 100 miss, and the long-run share is exactly 10%. At $z = 2.576$, the 99% multiplier, only 1 of these misses. Higher confidence costs width.

screens.prose: Push the other way. At $z = 3$ no line here misses, yet $P(|Z| > 3) = 0.0027$ for a normal.
screens.question: Which multiplier gives a 100% confidence interval?

options.text: No finite $z$: the interval must be the whole line

options.why: These 100 all catch $\mu$ at 3, but 27 in 10,000 backtests would still miss.
That is the 99% multiplier. One line in a hundred still misses on average.
Doubling $z$ does not reach certainty. A tail of about 0.0001 still misses.

hints.text: Does the normal curve ever reach zero height?
Any finite band leaves two tails outside it, however thin.
Only $(-\infty, \infty)$ leaves no tail at all.

feedback.correct: A 100% interval is the whole line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether any finite band leaves no tail outside it.

explain.text: The normal's tails never reach zero, so every finite $z$ misses sometimes. A 100% interval is $(-\infty, \infty)$: certain, and useless. Every useful interval trades some confidence for a usable width.

screens.prose: The 1.96 assumes we know $\sigma$. With 10 days we estimate it by $s$, and $(\bar X - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{10})$ follows a $t$ distribution with 9 degrees of freedom. The band is $\pm 1.96$ on that $t$; the dashed curve is the normal.
screens.question: Does $\bar x \pm 1.96\,s/\sqrt{10}$ still catch $\mu$ 95% of the time?

options.why: You kept the normal's 1.96. With $s$ in place of $\sigma$, the shaded area reads 0.918, not 0.95.
You read the $t$ as narrower. Its tails are fatter, so more of it lies outside $\pm 1.96$.

hints.text: Read the shaded area on the $t$ curve.
Compare the tails of the two curves.
The band holds 0.918, less than 0.95.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the probability under the $t$ curve between $-1.96$ and $1.96$.

explain.text: Estimating $\sigma$ adds noise, so the $t$ has fatter tails and $\pm 1.96$ holds only 0.918. With 9 degrees of freedom the 95% multiplier is 2.262. The testing course treats the $t$ in full; from about 30 observations the two multipliers nearly agree.

screens.prose: A colleague's 100-day backtest gives a 95% interval of 0.02% to 0.22% for the mean daily return. The chart shows 100 such intervals, from the strategy you watched earlier.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The method catches $\mu$ in 95% of samples; this interval either contains $\mu$ or it does not
95% of daily returns lie between 0.02% and 0.22%
options.why: You read the interval as a range for single days. Days spread about 1% either way; the interval is about the mean $\mu$.

options.text: There is a 95% chance that $\mu$ lies between 0.02% and 0.22%
options.why: You gave $\mu$ a probability. Here $\mu$ is fixed and the interval is random. That reading needs a prior, later in this level.

options.text: 95% of future 100-day means will lie between 0.02% and 0.22%
options.why: You centred future means on this sample. They centre on $\mu$, and this interval may sit off-centre.

hints.text: In the chart, what changes from one backtest to the next: $\mu$ or the interval?
The dashed line never moves. The lines do.
The 95% is a property of the method across samples, not of one interval.

feedback.correct: The 95% belongs to the method, not to one interval.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In the chart, $\mu$ stays put and the intervals move.

byKey.data: You read the interval as covering 95% of the data. It covers the mean $\mu$, and days are far more spread out.
byKey.prob: You read the interval as a probability statement about $\mu$. With $\mu$ fixed, this one interval either holds it or not.

explain.text: In the chart $\mu$ is one fixed line, and each backtest draws its own interval. About 95 in 100 catch it; any single one either does or does not. A probability for $\mu$ itself is the Bayesian reading, which needs a prior.

screens.prose: Every interval you built had the same shape: $$\bar x \pm z\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}, \qquad z = 1.645,\ 1.96,\ 2.576 \ \text{for}\ 90\%,\ 95\%,\ 99\%.$$ The confidence level is the long-run share of samples whose interval catches $\mu$.
screens.question: To halve the width of a 95% interval, how many observations do you need?

options.why: You expected the width to fall in line with $n$. It falls with $\sqrt n$, so doubling $n$ cuts it only by $\sqrt 2$.
Halving $z$ does halve the width, but the interval drops to about 67% confidence.

hints.text: Which part of the formula holds $n$?
The width is $2z\,s/\sqrt n$.
Halving $1/\sqrt n$ needs $\sqrt n$ to double, so $n$ must grow fourfold.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The width is $2z\,s/\sqrt n$; find what halves it at the same $z$.

explain.text: The width is $2z\,s/\sqrt n$. At fixed 95% confidence, halving it needs $\sqrt n$ to double, so $n$ quadruples. Precision is expensive.

screens.prose: Show the interval catches $\mu$ with probability 0.95. Before the data arrive, $\bar X$ is random, so the endpoints $\bar X \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$ are random too.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P\left(-1.96 \le \dfrac{\bar X - \mu}{\mathrm{SE}} \le 1.96\right) = 0.95$, the band you found on the normal
$P(\bar X - 1.96\,\mathrm{SE} \le \mu \le \bar X + 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}) = 0.95$, multiply by $-1$, which flips both inequalities

hints.text: Start from the statement about $\bar X$ you found with the slider.
Each line does one thing to all three parts of the inequality.
Scale by SE, subtract $\bar X$, then multiply by $-1$.

feedback.correct: Each line rewrites the same event.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the standard normal band and isolate $\mu$ one step at a time.

explain.text: Each line changes all three parts of the inequality the same way, so the event is unchanged. The last line has random endpoints and a fixed $\mu$. Once $\bar x$ is observed, nothing random is left.

screens.prose: A strategy's 250-day backtest shows a mean daily return of $\bar x = 0.08\%$, with sample sd $s = 1.2\%$. Before trading it, you want a 95% interval for its true mean $\mu$.
screens.question: Which is the 95% interval, and what does it tell you?

options.text: $-0.07\%$ to $0.23\%$: we cannot rule out no edge
$-0.07\%$ to $0.23\%$: the strategy has no edge
options.why: Zero is inside, but so is 0.2%. The interval cannot tell them apart, so it proves neither.
You divided $s$ by $n = 250$. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{250} \approx 15.8$.

options.text: $-2.27\%$ to $2.43\%$: far too wide to say anything
options.why: You used $s$ itself. That is the spread of single days; the mean's spread is $s/\sqrt n$.

hints.text: Find the standard error first.
Is the point marked 'no edge' inside your interval?
$\mathrm{SE} = 1.2/\sqrt{250} = 0.0759$, so the interval is $0.08 \pm 0.149$.

feedback.correct: Zero is inside the interval, so no edge is still plausible.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $0.08 \pm 1.96 \times 1.2/\sqrt{250}$, then check whether 0 is inside.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = 1.2/\sqrt{250} = 0.0759$, so the interval is $0.08 \pm 0.149$: from $-0.069\%$ to $0.229\%$. Zero is inside, so the backtest cannot rule out a strategy with no edge. It cannot rule out a good one either.

screens.prose: A fund's annualised volatility, estimated from 504 daily returns, is $\hat\sigma = 16\%$. The standard error of a volatility estimate is about $\hat\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$.
screens.question: What is the half-width of the 95% interval, in percentage points?

hints.text: Find the SE first, then multiply by 1.96.
The interval is centred on $\hat\sigma = 16\%$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\mathrm{SE} = 16/\sqrt{2 \times 504}$, then multiply by 1.96.

byKey.no-two: You used $\sqrt{n}$. A volatility estimate's SE has $\sqrt{2n}$ underneath.
byKey.one-se: That is one standard error. The 95% half-width is 1.96 of them.
byKey.sd-only: You multiplied 16 by 1.96. Divide by $\sqrt{2n}$ first.
byKey.decimal: 0.00988 is 0.988 points written as a decimal. Type the number of percentage points, 0.988.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = 16/\sqrt{1008} = 0.504$ points, so the half-width is $1.96 \times 0.504 = 0.99$. The 95% interval runs from about 15.0% to 17.0%. Two years pin a volatility down far better than a mean.

ideas: A 95% confidence interval is $\bar x \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$; use 1.645 for 90% and 2.576 for 99%.
The 95% is a property of the method: in repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals catch $\mu$.
With $\sigma$ estimated from a small sample, the $t$ multiplier is larger than 1.96.
summary.trap: A 95% interval does not hold 95% of the data. Nor does it give $\mu$ a 95% chance of being inside.

quiz.prose: A strategy won 55% of 400 trades. The standard error of a hit rate is $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$.
quiz.question: What is the lower end of the 95% interval for its true hit rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the SE, then step down 1.96 of them from 0.55.

byKey.one-se: You stepped down one SE. A 95% interval steps down 1.96.
byKey.sd: You used $\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}$ without dividing by $n$. That is the spread of one trade.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{0.2475/400} = 0.0249$, so the interval is $0.55 \pm 0.049$: about 50.1% to 59.9%. It only just excludes a coin flip.

quiz.prose: A desk builds a 95% interval for the mean return of each of 40 strategies. In truth, none of them has any edge, and the backtests are independent.
quiz.question: How many intervals would you expect to exclude zero?

widget.accept: 2: each misses the true mean, 0, with chance 0.05, and $40 \times 0.05 = 2$
widget.label: Expected number

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each interval misses the true mean with chance 0.05.

byKey.none: You expected no false alarms. Each interval misses its target 5% of the time, even with no edge.
byKey.thirty-eight: 38 is how many contain zero. The question asks for the ones that exclude it.

explain.text: Each interval excludes the true value 0 with chance 0.05. Over 40 independent strategies we expect $40 \times 0.05 = 2$ to look like they have an edge. Testing many strategies manufactures false discoveries.

quiz.prose: A 95% interval from 64 days is 0.5 percentage points wide.
quiz.question: About how wide is the 95% interval from 256 days, with a similar $s$?

options.why: You scaled the width with $n$. It scales with $1/\sqrt n$, and $\sqrt{256/64} = 2$.
The width depends on $n$ through $s/\sqrt n$. More days, narrower interval.
More data narrows an interval; it never widens it on average.

feedback.correct: Four times the data halves the width.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The width is proportional to $1/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: $256 = 4 \times 64$, and $\sqrt 4 = 2$. So the width halves, from 0.5 to 0.25 points.

quiz.prose: A backtest gives $\bar x = 0.12\%$ a day, with $\mathrm{SE} = 0.05\%$.
quiz.question: What is the upper end of the 99% interval, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 99% interval uses $z = 2.576$.

byKey.ninety-five: That is the 95% upper end. A 99% interval reaches further: $z = 2.576$.
byKey.decimal: 0.002488 is 0.2488% written as a decimal. The field asks for the number of per cent, so type 0.2488 without a % sign.

explain.text: $0.12 + 2.576 \times 0.05 = 0.2488$. The 99% interval, from $-0.009\%$ to $0.249\%$, now includes zero, while the 95% one did not.
